source.title: Offline memory replay in recurrent neuronal networks emerges from constraints on online dynamics.

confidence_rationale: A CA3 spiking-network model showing that biased (reward-salience-weighted) replay is an EMERGENT consequence of realistic network constraints: over-representation of salient/rewarded locations in the online code produces biased offline replay. Establishes substrate availability for MECH-443 -- prioritized replay does not need a bespoke priority module, it falls out of the population code. Substrate-availability anchor (like Joo&Frank for MECH-319), not a direct test of the write step, hence moderate-low confidence.
failure_signatures: Substrate-availability evidence: it shows reward-biased replay can emerge, not that the bias gates a downstream rule/value write.
Bias arises from over-representation of salient positions in the population code; if REE's rule layer is not over-representing high-utility rules analogously, the emergent route does not transfer.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Imposing experimentally-observed constraints (sparsity, selectivity, rhythmicity, adaptation, associative connectivity) on a CA3 recurrent network yields, as an emergent property, offline replay that is biased toward salient locations such as reward sites.
mapping.ree_translation: MECH-443: a graded, reward/salience-weighted priority over replayed content is biologically cheap -- it emerges from the structure of the population code rather than requiring a dedicated priority computation, so wiring a priority signal into REE's replay write channel rests on an available substrate.
mapping.mapping_caveat: This is a substrate-availability result: it shows biased replay can emerge from network constraints, not that the bias is read out as a write-strength onto a downstream rule-arbitration layer.
mapping.source_context: Recurrent spiking network model of hippocampal CA3 optimized to match observed dynamics during simulated spatial exploration.

confidence_components.notes: Good substrate-availability anchor; deliberately weighted below the function-level papers because it shows emergence of the bias, not its downstream use.
